cells.quote: For example, for Total Accuracy, as measured by Raw Score, ( ATOTACC)), the intercept from the growth curve model (reading level at 1 st grade) was predictive of accuracy scores in adulthood for both typical and dyslexic groups, although more strongly for typical readers (β0 = 0.980 and 0.473, for typical and dyslexic readers, respectively).
cells.note: The study reports a stronger association from first-grade reading level for typical readers, while the combined intercept-and-slope model explained more variance for dyslexic readers.

cells.quote: gains in reading were positively correlated with GMV in the left superior temporal gyrus (STG) at the age of 7.5 15

D.treatment: stronger GMV decreases in parietal and inferior frontal regions
D.comparison: weaker GMV decreases in those regions

O.outcome_detail: word decoding, reading fluency, and rapid automatized naming

cells.quote: In another study using a wider age range (initially 5 –15-year olds scanned twice in the course of two years), GMV decrease in parietal cortical and inferior frontal regions was also associated with better word decoding, reading ﬂuency, and rapid auto- mated naming16.
cells.note: The review reports an association between longitudinal GMV decrease and better reading-related outcomes; no printed effect size is given.

O.outcome_detail: fractional anisotropy in the left arcuate fasciculus and inferior longitudinal fasciculus

cells.quote: In line with this observation, children with above-average reading skills initially presented low FA of the left AF and ILF that increased over a 3 year period 22.
cells.note: The review reports a longitudinal increase in FA but does not provide a printed effect size or specify the comparison group.

O.outcome_detail: false recall of non-presented animal names

cells.quote: For example, football experts who studied lists of animal names that were also names of football teams later falsely recalled many non-presented animal names that represented football teams. This resulted in a higher number of falsely recalled words in experts than in non-experts, a pattern that was absent in a control task in which participants had to study body parts 14.
cells.note: The study text reports higher false recall for experts than non-experts, indicating more memory intrusions, but does not report an effect size, setting, duration, age, or assignment method.

D.comparison: hint provided afterward or not at all

cells.quote: Comprehension ratings and recall performance were strongly enhanced in participants who were given the hint beforehand, which provides evidence that available prior knowledge needs to be activated in order to affect learning.
cells.note: The commentary reports Bransford and Johnson's study; the setting, duration, assignment procedure, and effect size are not stated.

cells.quote: The paradox describes the ﬁnding that remembering a face –name association (i.e., that a person ’s surname is Baker) is disproportionately harder than remembering face –profession associations (i.e., that a person’s profession is baker).
cells.note: The commentary reports the Baker–baker paradox; the setting, duration, assignment procedure, timing, and effect size are not stated.

O.outcome_detail: false recall of non-presented animal names that were football-team names

cells.quote: Football experts who studied lists of animal names that were also names of football teams later falsely recalled many non-presented animal names that represented football teams. This resulted in a higher number of falsely recalled words in experts than in non-experts, a pattern that was absent in a control task in which participants had to study body parts 14.
cells.note: The comparison is based on pre-existing expertise groups; the commentary does not report an effect size or the study setting and duration.

O.outcome_detail: Reading levels from first through fifth grade

result.effect: Mean first-grade intercept 13.62 vs 6.92; mean slope 12.00 vs 13.10

cells.quote: The mean intercept represents the average reading level at 1 st grade, indicating large differences between both groups ( µ0 = 13.62 and 6.92, for typical and dyslexic readers, respectively). The mean slope denotes the mean overall increase in reading scores from 1 st through 5th grade (µs = 12.00 and 13.10, for typical and dyslexic readers, respectively). Given the large discrepancy in reading levels at 1 st grade between typical and dyslexic readers together with their similar increases over the five grades, the reading levels at 5 th grade remain disproportionate between both groups.
cells.note: The groups were observed longitudinally; no intervention was assigned.

O.outcome_detail: Adult reading accuracy, comprehension, and speed at average age 42

result.effect: Adult means: ATOTACC 27.48 vs 12.58; ATOTCOMP 12.70 vs 9.76; AAVGSPEED 144.36 vs 120.7; STOTCOMP 14.40 vs 11.65; SAVGSECS 96.21 vs 121.5

cells.quote: Across all measures, both grade school and adult reading, typical readers have higher means than dyslexic readers (Note that SAVGSECS is time needed to read a passage. Thus, higher values indicate slower reading).
cells.note: For SAVGSECS, the typical-reader mean is better because lower reading time indicates faster reading.

O.outcome_detail: Adult reading outcomes predicted by first-to-fifth-grade reading trajectory

result.effect: Slope βs for ATOTCOMP 0.567 vs 0.280; STOTCOMP 0.519 vs 0.199; SAVGSECS −0.355 vs −0.078; R2 for ATOTCOMP 0.361 vs 0.101 and STOTCOMP 0.353 vs 0.180

cells.quote: The relations from the slope, however, were weaker (or nonsigni ﬁcant) for typical readers but remained strong for dyslexic readers. For example, for Total Comprehension, as measured by Raw Score ( ATOTCOMP), the relation from reading levels at 1 st grade were equivalent for both groups ( β0 = 0.545). In contrast, whereas the relation from the slope decreased for typical readers ( βs = 0.280), it increased for dyslexic readers ( βs = 0.567). In other words, reading level in 1 st grade was associated with comprehension scores in adulthood similarly for both groups. However, the trajectory of children ’s reading development from 1st to 5 th grade was strongly related to adult comprehension scores for dyslexic, but not as much for typical readers.
cells.note: The contrast concerns the strength of the measured association, not a randomized treatment effect.

O.outcome_detail: Adult silent comprehension and silent reading speed predicted by reading trajectory

result.effect: STOTCOMP slope βs 0.519 vs 0.199 (typical p=0.058); SAVGSECS slope βs −0.355 vs −0.078 (typical p=0.480)

cells.quote: Similarly, whereas the relation from the slope decreased for typical readers ( βs = 0.280), it increased for dyslexic readers ( βs = 0.567). In other words, reading level in 1 st grade was associated with comprehension scores in adulthood similarly for both groups. However, the trajectory of children ’s reading development from 1st to 5 th grade was strongly related to adult comprehension scores for dyslexic, but not as much for typical readers. Although this pattern was true for all remaining outcomes, it was even more pronounced for silent reading comprehension, as measured by raw score ( STOTCOMP), and Average Seconds to Read Passages during silent reading, as measured by Raw Score ( SAVGSECS), for which the prediction from the slope was not statistically signiﬁcant for typical readers ( βs = 0.199 and −0.078, p > 0.05), but remained high for dyslexic readers ( βs = 0.519 and –0.355, p < 0.05).
cells.note: The study reports stronger predictive associations for dyslexic readers; the nonsignificant typical-reader estimates are not coded as equivalence.

O.outcome_detail: mean reading-speed increase after lexical categorization training

cells.quote: The best-performing pipeline increased reading speed from 23% in the unselected group to 43% in the machine-selected group.
